header:
Date: 2025-07-02
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 56m
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lina Zhou (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Aurora CTO), Evan Cho (Aurora ML), Sara Lim (Aurora PM), Tom Baker (Aurora Ops)
Recording: enabled

summary: POC scoping focused on unit economics (per-token estimates), batching and KV cache knobs, and benchmarking plan. Customer has a 1500 qps peak target for a chat-like assistant with average 120 tokens per request; budget discussions centered on ~ $15k/month initially. Agreed next steps: run 1k-request benchmark, share cost spreadsheet, and schedule security deep dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call. We want to lock down the POC success criteria and do a quick cost run-through.
[00:22] Priya (Aurora): Hi, thanks. We're mostly here to understand unit economics and whether Redwood can meet our latency SLO at scale without blowing our budget.
[00:35] Diego (Redwood): Great. Quick note — apologies in advance, my audio is a little echo-y. We'll circle on benchmarks: can you confirm typical prompt lengths and 95th percentile latency target?
[00:48] Evan (Aurora): Average is around 120 tokens per request, with some longer threads up to 600 tokens. We care about p95 under 400ms for assistant responses.
[01:02] Lina (Redwood): Understood. For that workload we usually size based on peak QPS and average seq len; you said peaks are about 1500 qps?
[01:15] Priya: Peak concurrent requests translate to roughly 1200-1500 QPS in spike events. Daily active is lower. Budget-wise we want to cap to roughly $15k/mo for initial POC — that's a hard guardrail.
[01:30] Diego: Ok that budget will heavily determine whether a hosted plan or a small Dedicated pool makes sense. Quick back-of-envelope: at 120 tokens per request and 1k steady qps, that's ~3.6M tokens/minute, math-ish. We need to model per-token cost with batching and KV prefix cache.
[01:52] Sara (Aurora): Can you explain how batching helps vs cache? We have lots of repeated prompts with small personalization.
[02:05] Diego: Sure — batching reduces per-token overhead by amortizing kernel launches; effective for synchronous calls. KV/prefix cache is for repeated prefixes: if many users hit similar system prompt or common preamble, you avoid re-computing kv for that prefix which saves both latency and tokens. It's workload-dependent.
[02:32] Tom (Aurora): We're also evaluating private deployment (VPC) vs hosted. Is there a big cost delta?
[02:40] Maya: Private/Dedicated tends to have higher fixed cost (reserved GPU pools) but lower variable per-token rates if you have sustained throughput. Hosted is flexible but per-token premiums apply. We'll put numbers in the playbook.
[03:00] Priya: Important: SOC2 + key management. We use a customer-managed KMS.
[03:08] Lina: Redwood supports CMEK/HSM via integrations; we'll include the compliance sheet in the follow-up.
[03:18] Diego: On benchmarking cadence — propose three test axes: 1) latency at target SLO with representative prompts, 2) throughput ramp (qps to saturation), 3) cost per 1M tokens under different configs (no batching, batch=64, quantized model).
[03:38] Evan: For quantization, what accuracy hit should we expect? We can't have hallucination regressions.
[03:45] Diego: Typically int8 quantization for autoregressive is <2% quality delta on average but varies by eval set. We'll run your eval prompts and show rouge/accuracy delta.
[03:58] Priya: Can you give us a quick per-token example today? Even rough.
[04:05] Maya: Rough today: hosted baseline say $0.00018 per prompt-token and $0.00012 per response-token — but unit math varies. If you move to Dedicated with reserved capacity it could drop 25–45% depending on commitment and batching. These are just illustrative numbers; we'll run exact on your corpora.
[04:30] Sara: If we do heavy caching, how does that change cost?
[04:36] Diego: Caching can reduce token compute by 30–70% for assistant workflows with repeated context. Example: a 40% effective cache hit rate at p95 reduces compute tokens by ~40% which flows linearly to token cost, plus latency improvement.
[04:56] Priya: We need a scenario analysis: best/worst/expected costs per month for 300k active users, 1500 peak qps.
[05:06] Maya: We'll produce a scenario spreadsheet — low/medium/high assumptions for cache hit, batching efficiency, quantization.
[05:15] Tom: Network egress — is that charged by Redwood? We need to know egress on Private.
[05:21] Lina: For Hosted, egress is usually in your cloud bill; Redwood can help estimate based on token sizes. For Private, you'll manage egress. We'll note that in the cost sheet.
[05:38] Evan: Can we run an initial 1k-request benchmark with these prompts and have Redwood provide CSVs with per-request latency and token counts?
[05:46] Diego: Yes — we'll run 1k synthetic + 1k replay of your sample prompts. That'll include latency distribution and token billing simulation across configs.
[06:00] Priya: Timeline question — how long to get a realistic number?
[06:05] Maya: If you provide prompts and traffic histogram this week, we can run benchmarks and share results in 5 business days. Security follow-up can be scheduled after that.
[06:20] Evan: We'll need exact metric definitions: p50/p95/p99 request latency, tokenized input/output counts, GPU utilization, and cost per million tokens.
[06:30] Diego: We'll include those fields in the CSV. Also we'll include notes for how we calculate tokenization (we use BPE-like token counts and will provide tokenizer outputs).
[06:45] Sara: What about peak blocking? If we spike to 1500 and we provision Dedicated for 1k, what's the fallback?
[06:52] Maya: We recommend routing policy with graceful fallback to a cheaper hosted variant; Redwood's smart routing can spill to burst capacity, but you'll see higher variable cost during spill. We'll model that too.
[07:08] Priya: For success criteria: 1) p95 < 400ms for 95% of traffic, 2) cost per MAU below X (we'll define), 3) security sign-off. Can we capture that?
[07:18] Maya: Yes. We'll formalize SLOs in the POC doc.
[07:26] Tom: A quick note — our KMS is AWS KMS with a bring-your-key policy.
[07:32] Lina: Good — Redwood supports CMEK; we'll include HSM/KMS integration details and required audit logs.
[07:40] Evan: On the benchmarking variants — please include: hosted baseline (optimized kernels), dedicated unquantized, dedicated int8 quantized, and a batch-optimized path.
[07:52] Diego: Will do. Also we'll measure memory/KV cache hit rates to show savings.
[08:00] Priya: How do you simulate user behavior? We have both chat sessions and single-turn completions.
[08:06] Diego: We'll run two workload profiles: session-oriented with prefix caching (simulates threading) and single-turn high-throughput. That shows cache benefits.
[08:18] Sara: Anything we should prepare beyond prompts/histograms?
[08:22] Maya: Also share a few representative failing prompts you care about — that helps us measure regression risk if we quantize.
[08:31] Priya: Noted.
[08:35] Diego: Side note — we might recommend smaller batching for low-latency critical paths and larger batch for background re-rankers. We'll include recommendations.
[08:45] Evan: For the cost model spreadsheet, can you include amortized GPU cost per token and also show CDN/egress where applicable?
[08:52] Maya: Yes — both compute and network line items will be included.
[09:00] Tom: Security follow-up attendees should include our SecOps and legal.
[09:05] Lina: We'll bring Redwood's security lead.
[09:09] Priya: Last question — any recommended acceptance tests for quality after quantization?
[09:15] Diego: We'll run your eval set and flag any prompts with >x% drop in key metrics (we'll agree threshold). Also run A/B for 10k conversations.
[09:29] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps: Aurora provides prompts + histogram; Redwood runs 1k synthetic + 1k replay benchmark across 4 configs; Redwood shares CSV + cost spreadsheet + security checklist; schedule security deep dive.
[09:48] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:52] Sara: Thanks.
[09:54] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites.
[56:00] (call ends)
